title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 75–76
description: Curated compound nouns, spelling and stress patterns, grammar and phrasal-verb-based noun expressions with original contextual examples.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow the source topics and relevant exercise vocabulary; explanations and example sentences are newly written. Original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Checked complete teaching pages, vocabulary tables, compound spelling and grammar notes, exercise prompts, illustrations where relevant, and corresponding answer-key entries for Units 75–76.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is provided when confidently transcribed; uncertain longer expressions omit IPA. Main-stress, spelling and countability notes reflect the study pages; exhaustive regional variants are not represented.
audit.languagePolicy: All teaching content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared learning targets, illustrations and relevant exercises against the supplied book and answer key; checked lexical meaning, context, articles, register, IPA where supplied and audio target suitability; validated local JSON structure and unique IDs.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio; no live VocabLab browser import, TTS or speech-recognition test was performed.

units.title: Unit 75 — Compound nouns 1: noun + noun
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 75. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise open, closed and hyphenated compound nouns, and note unpredictable spelling variation.
Identify typical primary-stress patterns of familiar compound nouns.
Use compound nouns with appropriate countability, article and plural patterns.
Recognise key compound nouns for money, health, transport, social issues and daily life, including exercise targets.

sectionsChecked: B: How are compound nouns written?
D: Grammar of compound nouns; singular and plural patterns

items.example: A compound noun can contain two words but name just one idea.
items.note: A fixed noun expression made up of more than one element; spelling is not always predictable.
items.section: A · What compound nouns are

items.example: The conference has a car park behind the main building.
items.note: British English; American English usually uses parking lot.
items.section: A · What compound nouns are

items.example: Every human being deserves to be treated with dignity.
items.note: A countable compound meaning a person; plural human beings.
items.section: A · What compound nouns are

items.example: She enjoys science fiction about distant planets.
items.note: Usually uncountable when naming the literary or film genre.
items.section: A · What compound nouns are

items.example: Could you pass me the tin opener, please?
items.note: British term for an implement that opens food tins; can opener is also common.
items.section: B · Open, hyphenated and closed compounds

items.example: Please check that your bank account details are correct.
items.note: A countable open compound: bank accounts.
items.section: B · Open, hyphenated and closed compounds

items.pt: faixa de pedestres; travessia de pedestres
items.example: We stopped at the pedestrian crossing to let people pass.
items.note: A marked place where people cross a road; a countable open compound.
items.section: B · Open, hyphenated and closed compounds

items.example: Staying calm during the disagreement required self-control.
items.note: Normally uncountable and often written with a hyphen.
items.section: B · Open, hyphenated and closed compounds

items.example: She lost an earring on the train.
items.note: A countable closed compound, written as one word.
items.section: B · Open, hyphenated and closed compounds

items.example: The company registered a new trademark for its software.
items.note: Written as one word; can mean a legal mark or a distinctive feature.
items.section: B · Open, hyphenated and closed compounds

items.example: We hired a babysitter for Saturday evening.
items.note: A countable closed compound for someone who looks after children temporarily.
items.section: B · Open, hyphenated and closed compounds

items.example: My alarm clock rang before sunrise.
items.note: Countable; the main stress usually falls on alarm.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: I dropped a contact lens while getting ready.
items.note: Countable; commonly used in the plural, contact lenses.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: Would you prefer still or sparkling mineral water?
items.note: Usually uncountable as a liquid; a bottle of mineral water is countable.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.pt: correio de voz; mensagem de voz
items.example: I left a message on his voice mail.
items.note: Also written voicemail; a phone message system or messages stored there.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.pt: doador de sangue; doadora de sangue
items.example: The hospital urgently needs more blood donors.
items.note: Countable compound naming a person who gives blood.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: She paid for the ticket with her credit card.
items.note: Countable; credit is the modifier and card is the head noun.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: They booked a package holiday that included flights and accommodation.
items.note: British English; a holiday sold with transport and accommodation included.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: The driver cleaned the windscreen before setting off.
items.note: British English; American English typically uses windshield.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: The burglar alarm went off during the night.
items.note: A device that detects or warns of unauthorised entry.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: His grandfather recovered well after a heart attack.
items.note: Countable medical event; have a heart attack.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: Keep both hands on the steering wheel when driving.
items.note: The wheel used to control the direction of a vehicle.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: One windscreen wiper stopped working during the storm.
items.note: Countable; often windscreen wipers in the plural for a vehicle.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: Let's meet at the bus stop opposite the station.
items.note: Countable; a designated stopping place for buses.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: We replaced the broken light bulb in the hallway.
items.note: A countable light source; plural light bulbs.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.pt: sachê de chá; saquinho de chá
items.example: Leave the tea bag in the cup for two minutes.
items.note: Countable; a small bag containing tea leaves.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: We stayed at a youth hostel near the old town.
items.note: Budget accommodation often used by travellers.
items.section: C · Common countable compounds and stress

items.example: Air traffic control instructed the aircraft to wait.
items.note: Usually uncountable when referring to the service or activity.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.example: The health centre provides information about birth control.
items.note: Uncountable term for preventing pregnancy.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.example: The nurse checked my blood pressure twice.
items.note: Normally uncountable; say high or low blood pressure.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.pt: tecnologia da computação; tecnologia de computadores
items.example: Advances in computer technology have changed medical imaging.
items.note: Usually an uncountable field of technology, though technologies can be counted individually.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.example: She used cotton wool to clean the small mark.
items.note: British English; refers to soft cotton used for cleaning or medical purposes.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.example: The team automated much of the data processing.
items.note: Usually uncountable; refers to processing information.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.example: Several guests developed food poisoning after the meal.
items.note: Usually uncountable; illness caused by contaminated food.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.pt: rinite alérgica ao pólen; alergia ao pólen
items.example: Her hay fever becomes worse in the spring.
items.note: Uncountable; allergy often caused by airborne pollen.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.example: Most employees pay income tax through their salaries.
items.note: Usually uncountable when referring to the type of tax.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.example: Eating junk food every day may leave little room for a balanced diet.
items.note: Uncountable; a broad informal term for food of poor nutritional quality.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.example: The company began as a mail order business.
items.note: Typically a modifier or an uncountable shopping method.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.example: The children saved their pocket money for a new game.
items.note: British English, normally uncountable; often money given to children to spend.
items.section: D · Compounds usually treated as uncountable

items.example: The two countries tried to avoid a new arms race.
items.note: The book groups this with compounds used in singular form; often preceded by an article.
items.section: D · Compounds presented in singular patterns

items.example: Climate change is affecting farming in many regions.
items.note: Usually uncountable when referring to the global process.
items.section: D · Compounds presented in singular patterns

items.example: The country abolished the death penalty years ago.
items.note: Often the death penalty when referring to capital punishment as an institution.
items.section: D · Compounds presented in singular patterns

items.example: Their conversations revealed a generation gap between parents and teenagers.
items.note: A difference in attitudes or expectations between generations.
items.section: D · Compounds presented in singular patterns

items.pt: força de trabalho; população economicamente ativa
items.example: Many skilled workers joined the local labour force.
items.note: British spelling labour; the total group of people available for work.
items.section: D · Compounds presented in singular patterns

items.example: The aircraft was designed to break the sound barrier.
items.note: Usually the sound barrier in the expression break the sound barrier.
items.section: D · Compounds presented in singular patterns

items.example: The debate focused on how to fund the welfare state.
items.note: A system in which the state provides social support and public services.
items.section: D · Compounds presented in singular patterns

items.pt: base de um movimento; pessoas comuns da base
items.example: The campaign gained support at the grass roots.
items.note: Usually plural when referring to ordinary supporters or local-level involvement.
items.section: D · Compounds often used in plural forms

items.example: She put on her headphones before joining the call.
items.note: Usually a plural noun; a pair of headphones.
items.section: D · Compounds often used in plural forms

items.example: These kitchen scissors are ideal for cutting herbs.
items.note: Scissors is plural in form; say a pair of kitchen scissors.
items.section: D · Compounds often used in plural forms

items.pt: artigos de luxo; bens de luxo
items.example: Demand for luxury goods remained strong despite higher prices.
items.note: The book presents this in the plural; luxury good can refer to one item.
items.section: D · Compounds often used in plural forms

items.pt: relações raciais; relações entre grupos raciais
items.example: The report examines race relations in the region.
items.note: Normally plural; relations between people of different racial backgrounds.
items.section: D · Compounds often used in plural forms

items.example: Roadworks caused delays on the motorway.
items.note: British English; normally plural in form, usually with a plural verb.
items.section: D · Compounds often used in plural forms

items.example: I left my sunglasses in the car.
items.note: Plural noun; a pair of sunglasses.
items.section: D · Compounds often used in plural forms

items.example: Turn left at the next set of traffic lights.
items.note: Usually plural for the signalling equipment at a junction; a traffic light can mean one signal.
items.section: D · Compounds often used in plural forms

items.example: The filters blocked most of the junk mail.
items.note: Normally uncountable; unsolicited letters, especially advertising.
items.section: E · Exercise-only compound nouns

items.pt: frase curta de efeito; trecho curto de declaração
items.example: The journalist used a brief soundbite from the minister's interview.
items.note: A short, memorable statement used in the media; often written as one word.
items.section: E · Exercise-only compound nouns

items.example: Blood ties were not the only reason they stayed close.
items.note: Plural noun for family relationships, especially biological ones.
items.section: E · Exercise-only compound nouns

items.example: They served hot tea from a large ceramic teapot.
items.note: A countable closed compound.
items.section: E · Exercise-only compound nouns

items.pt: país de origem; pátria de origem
items.example: She still feels connected to her mother country.
items.note: The country someone regards as their homeland or ancestral origin.
items.section: E · Exercise-only compound nouns

items.pt: imposto sobre herança; imposto sobre transmissão hereditária
items.example: The heirs asked an accountant about inheritance tax.
items.note: Tax payable in some jurisdictions when property is inherited.
items.section: E · Exercise-only compound nouns

items.pt: processamento de texto; edição de textos
items.example: The course includes basic word-processing skills.
items.note: Often hyphenated before another noun; also written word processing.
items.section: E · Exercise-only compound nouns

items.pt: passagem de nível; cruzamento ferroviário em nível
items.example: The barriers were lowered at the level crossing.
items.note: British English; a road crossing railway tracks at the same level.
items.section: E · Exercise-only compound nouns

items.example: We chose fast food because we had only a short lunch break.
items.note: Normally uncountable when referring to a type of food.
items.section: E · Exercise-only compound nouns

items.pt: competição desgastante do dia a dia; rotina competitiva
items.example: He left the corporate rat race to work independently.
items.note: Informal; an exhausting and highly competitive routine.
items.section: E · Exercise-only compound nouns

units.title: Unit 76 — Compound nouns 2: verb + preposition
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 76. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise compound nouns derived from phrasal verbs, their meanings and plural forms.
Use journalistic, business, technological and everyday compound nouns in original contexts.
Distinguish multiple senses such as turnover and fallout and typical prepositions with compounds.
Differentiate similar-looking word-order pairs, including outlook/look-out, set-up/upset and outlay/layout.

sectionsChecked: A: Compound nouns based on phrasal verbs

items.pt: aquisição de empresa; tomada de controle
items.example: The proposed takeover would create a much larger company.
items.note: From take over; gaining control of another business, often through purchase.
items.section: A · Nouns formed from phrasal verbs

items.example: I usually do a short workout after work.
items.note: Countable noun from work out; plural workouts.
items.section: A · Nouns formed from phrasal verbs

items.example: Workers organised a walkout after negotiations failed.
items.note: From walk out; often a short strike or coordinated departure in protest.
items.section: B · Journalism and public events

items.example: The council announced a crackdown on illegal dumping.
items.note: From crack down on; forceful measures against an activity, usually crackdown on.
items.section: B · Journalism and public events

items.example: Officials investigated the breakout from the high-security prison.
items.note: From break out; a prison escape or sudden emergence depending on context.
items.section: B · Journalism and public events

items.example: The department underwent a management shake-up.
items.note: From shake up; major changes in organisation or personnel.
items.section: B · Journalism and public events

items.example: Their break-up came as a surprise to their friends.
items.note: From break up; collapse of a relationship or organisation.
items.section: B · Journalism and public events

items.example: The manufacturer opened a new retail outlet near the airport.
items.note: A place selling products in the unit; it can also mean an exit for air, water or energy. Do not confuse with a let-out (a means of escape).
items.section: C · Business and the economy

items.pt: caixa de supermercado; área de pagamento
items.example: There was a long queue at the check-out.
items.note: From check out; a place to pay for goods. Also checkout as one word.
items.section: C · Business and the economy

items.pt: corte; redução de gastos ou recursos
items.example: The organisation announced a cutback in travel spending.
items.note: From cut back; often a cutback in or on spending.
items.section: C · Business and the economy

items.example: The business reported higher turnover than last year.
items.note: Business sense: sales value over a period; also staff changes in employment contexts.
items.section: C · Business and the economy

items.example: The government approved a bailout for the struggling bank.
items.note: Money or support intended to prevent financial failure.
items.section: C · Business and the economy

items.example: The program rejected an invalid input.
items.note: Information or material put into a system; also ideas contributed by people.
items.section: D · Technology and modern life

items.example: The system's output was saved to a log file.
items.note: What a process or system produces; can be data or goods.
items.section: D · Technology and modern life

items.example: The company reduced staff turnover by improving working conditions.
items.note: Rate at which employees leave and are replaced, not company sales turnover.
items.section: D · Technology and modern life

items.pt: pessoa que abandona estudos ou grupo; desistente
items.example: The college introduced a programme to support students at risk of becoming dropouts.
items.note: From drop out; the textbook also describes someone rejecting conventional society.
items.section: D · Technology and modern life

items.example: Radioactive fallout contaminated the surrounding fields.
items.note: From fall out; radioactive material, or figuratively negative consequences.
items.section: D · Technology and modern life

items.example: Could you bring a printout of the latest results?
items.note: From print out; paper copy of computer information.
items.section: D · Technology and modern life

items.example: Researchers reported a breakthrough in battery technology.
items.note: An important discovery or progress, often a breakthrough in a field.
items.section: D · Technology and modern life

items.example: A breakdown in communication delayed the project.
items.note: From break down; failure of a machine, system or relationship.
items.section: E · Everyday and general meanings

items.example: The economic outlook remains uncertain.
items.note: Future prospects; can also refer to weather forecasts or a personal attitude.
items.section: E · Everyday and general meanings

items.example: The main drawback of this design is its high power consumption.
items.note: A negative aspect; often drawback of something.
items.section: E · Everyday and general meanings

items.example: We will evaluate the outcome of the experiment next week.
items.note: Final result of a process, discussion or event.
items.section: E · Everyday and general meanings

items.example: The trainees gave useful feedback on the workshop.
items.note: Usually uncountable; comments that help assess or improve something.
items.section: E · Everyday and general meanings

items.example: The costs were clear from the outset.
items.note: Common fixed expression from the outset, meaning from the beginning.
items.section: E · Everyday and general meanings

items.example: The new laboratory set-up allows safer testing.
items.note: Organisation, arrangement or configuration; also written setup.
items.section: E · Everyday and general meanings

items.pt: recuo para parada; área de parada à margem da estrada
items.example: We pulled into a lay-by to check the map.
items.note: British English; a small stopping place beside a road.
items.section: E · Everyday and general meanings

items.example: The new bypass reduced traffic through the town centre.
items.note: A road built to avoid a busy urban area; also a medical term elsewhere.
items.section: E · Everyday and general meanings

items.example: Officials reported an outbreak of influenza in the region.
items.note: Sudden start of disease, violence or another undesirable event.
items.section: E · Everyday and general meanings

items.pt: fila de veículos; congestionamento em fila
items.example: The crash caused a long tailback on the motorway.
items.note: British English; a queue of traffic stretching back from an obstruction.
items.section: F · Additional nouns from exercises

items.example: Police investigated a break-in at the warehouse.
items.note: Countable illegal entry into a building; from break in.
items.section: F · Additional nouns from exercises

items.example: The investigation uncovered a cover-up of the safety failures.
items.note: From cover up; deliberate attempt to conceal facts.
items.section: F · Additional nouns from exercises

items.example: Losing the prototype was a serious setback for the project.
items.note: From set back; obstacle that delays progress.
items.section: F · Additional nouns from exercises

items.example: Heavy traffic caused a hold-up on the bridge.
items.note: From hold up; here a delay. Another sense is an armed robbery.
items.section: F · Additional nouns from exercises

items.example: The thieves used a motorcycle for their getaway.
items.note: From get away; an escape, or an enjoyable short holiday in another context.
items.section: F · Additional nouns from exercises

items.example: The charity event attracted a large turnout.
items.note: From turn out; number of people who attend or participate.
items.section: F · Additional nouns from exercises

items.pt: dormir até mais tarde; manhã de descanso na cama
items.example: I enjoyed a lie-in on Sunday after a busy week.
items.note: British English; remaining in bed later than usual, from lie in.
items.section: F · Additional nouns from exercises

items.example: The speaker provided a handout with useful diagrams.
items.note: From hand out; a printed sheet for an audience, or something given free.
items.section: F · Additional nouns from exercises

items.pt: limpeza geral com descarte de objetos
items.example: We had a clear-out of the storage cupboard.
items.note: From clear out; removing unnecessary things from a place.
items.section: F · Additional nouns from exercises

items.example: A look-out watched the entrance while the others worked.
items.note: A person watching for danger; different from outlook, which means prospect.
items.section: G · Contrasting word order and meaning

items.example: The last-minute cancellation caused considerable upset.
items.note: As a noun, disturbance or distress; not the same as set-up.
items.section: G · Contrasting word order and meaning

items.example: They searched for a let-out clause in the contract.
items.note: A way to escape a difficult obligation; uncommon compared with the verb phrase.
items.section: G · Contrasting word order and meaning

items.example: The initial outlay for the equipment was considerable.
items.note: Money spent, especially at the start of an activity; contrasts with layout.
items.section: G · Contrasting word order and meaning

items.example: The document's layout makes the charts easy to follow.
items.note: How something is arranged in space or on a page; contrasts with outlay.
items.section: G · Contrasting word order and meaning
